post_title: Why People Seek Help, and What They Actually Need From It
post_content:
There is a gap between why someone walks into a helping relationship and what they actually need once they are there. In more than four decades of teaching and researching the helping process, I have come to believe that closing that gap is the real work of the skilled helper. Most people arrive carrying a story. What they need is someone willing to help them understand it.

#### What Brings Someone to a Helper

The reasons people seek help are rarely as straightforward as they appear. A person might say they are struggling with anxiety, or a relationship breakdown, or a career that no longer makes sense. And all of that is true. But underneath the presenting concern, there is almost always something less named: a sense that they are stuck in a pattern they cannot see clearly enough to change.

People seek help, in my experience, not because they are broken, but because they have reached the limit of what they can do alone. That is not a failure. It is a remarkably human recognition.

Most of us can sustain our own navigation through familiar territory. When the terrain shifts and the old maps stop working, we look for someone who can help us read the ground.

The mistake a helper can make at this point is to rush toward solving the problem as it was presented. The presenting problem is rarely the whole story. It is the door. What the client actually needs is someone willing to open it with them, not someone who has already decided what is on the other side.

Consider a man who arrives saying he wants help managing his temper at work. That is a real problem and it deserves attention.

But if the helper begins there, with techniques for managing anger, they may never learn that the temper appeared eighteen months ago, that it coincided with a promotion he did not want and could not refuse, and that what he is actually living with is a slow, unspoken sense that he has agreed to a life he did not choose. The anger is a symptom of something the man himself has not yet put into words. A helper who solves the presenting problem here has solved the wrong problem competently.

#### The Three Things Clients Are Usually Asking For

Across a great many helping relationships, I have come to think that what people are asking for, underneath whatever they say, tends to fall into three categories, and it is useful for a helper to know which one is in the room.

The first is clarity. The person cannot see their own situation well enough to act on it. Too many things are tangled together, or one thing is so large that it obscures everything around it. What they need is not advice but the experience of laying it out in front of someone who will help them see the shape of it.

The second is permission. The person often already knows what they want to do, and what they lack is the sense that it is legitimate to want it. This is more common than most helpers expect.

They are not looking for a decision. They are looking for the experience of saying the thing out loud to someone who does not immediately argue them out of it.

The third is capability. The person knows what they want and believes they are allowed to want it, and genuinely does not know how to get there. This is the only one of the three where anything resembling instruction is appropriate, and it is the least common of the three at the point of first contact, though helpers frequently treat it as the default.

Reading which of these is present, and not assuming, is one of the more consequential judgements in early helping.

#### What Clients Actually Need

If I had to name the one thing clients need from a helper, it would be this: the experience of being genuinely understood before anything else happens.

Not reassured. Not advised. Not redirected. Understood.

There is a passage in *The Skilled Helper* where I describe what a good helper makes possible: not the heroic intervention, not the transformative breakthrough, but the quieter thing, which is a relationship in which the client feels safe enough to look honestly at their own situation. That safety is not a soft precondition to the real work. It is the real work, in its early and most critical form.

Clients who feel understood are more likely to explore honestly. They are more willing to surface the things they have been avoiding, to name the beliefs that are keeping them stuck, to consider possibilities they had ruled out.

The client who feels managed or assessed or corrected tends to do the opposite. They perform. They present the version of themselves they think the helper wants to see.

This is why I hold the view that empathy is not a therapeutic technique. It is a stance, and it shapes everything that follows.

#### Why This Matters for How We Help

If what clients need first is to be understood, then the helper's primary discipline in the early stages of any helping relationship is not problem-solving. It is careful, unhurried listening, and the ability to communicate what has been heard in a way that shows the client they have been met.

This has practical consequences. A helper who moves too quickly to action planning, who introduces goals before the client's story has been properly heard, will often find that the action plan does not stick. Not because the plan is wrong, but because the client did not feel understood well enough to fully own it.

It also changes how a helper thinks about time. A session spent entirely on exploration, with no plan produced and no action agreed, can look from the outside like a session in which nothing happened. It is frequently the session that makes everything after it possible. Helpers under pressure to demonstrate progress are pushed toward the visible and away from the foundational, and the cost of that pressure is usually paid three or four sessions later, when a well-designed plan quietly fails to be enacted.

The structure I have described in *The Skilled Helper* is not a system to follow mechanically. It is a map for a human process. The map is useful precisely because it keeps the helper oriented toward the client's needs rather than their own need to feel helpful.

#### What to Do With This

If you are working as a helper, or developing toward that work, I would invite you to sit with one question: in your recent helping conversations, how much time passed before you moved from listening to advising?

Not because advising is always wrong. But because the ratio often reveals where the pressure is. When we move quickly, it is frequently our discomfort with sitting in another person's uncertainty, rather than a genuine signal that the client is ready to move.

The discipline of slowing down, of staying with the client's experience a little longer than feels comfortable, is one of the most transferable skills in this work. It is also, in my observation, one of the least practiced. It costs nothing to try in your next conversation, and it tends to reveal quickly how much you had been supplying that the other person had not asked for.

If you want to develop your understanding of the helping process, and the disciplines that make it genuinely useful, [The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan)](/academy/life-coaching/skilled-helper/) applies the model I have developed across a 7+ hour curriculum, covering the full arc from first contact to closure. Over 3,600 students have worked through it, and it sits within [the School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping](/academy/life-coaching/).

post_title: Listening Is Not Waiting to Speak: The Discipline of Tuning In
post_content:
Most people who enter a helping role believe they are good listeners. My experience, after a lifetime of training helpers and studying the helping process, is that most of us are not nearly as good at it as we think. Listening well is one of the most demanding disciplines in human communication, and it is almost never taught.

#### What Listening Actually Requires

When I describe listening in *The Skilled Helper*, I use the phrase tuning in. Not because it is poetic, but because it names something precise. Tuning in means attending to the whole person, not only the words. It means tracking the feelings behind the language, the things being avoided as well as the things being said, the way a sentence trails off or a topic is abandoned.

Most helpers listen at the level of content. They hear what is said and begin forming a response.

What they miss is the register. They miss the slight hesitation before a particular word. They miss the way energy drops when a subject is raised. They miss the moment when someone stops telling their story and starts performing it.

Listening at this level takes practice, and it takes something else too: the willingness to hold your own response in reserve. The urge to reply is strong. For many of us in helping roles, it is connected to something that feels like care, because we want to be useful, and responding feels like usefulness. But the discipline of tuning in asks something harder: to stay with the client's experience rather than moving toward our own.

#### The Three Layers of What Is Being Said

It helps to think of any client's account as arriving in three layers, each of which can be listened to and any of which can be missed.

The first layer is the content: the events, the people, the sequence of what happened. This is the layer almost everyone hears, and it is the layer most helpers can accurately summarise afterwards.

The second layer is the feeling: what the events meant to the person, what they are still carrying about them, what emotion sits underneath the recounting. This layer is often not stated directly. It appears in emphasis, in what gets repeated, in what is described in unusual detail and what is skipped over quickly. A person who describes a difficult meeting minute by minute and then says "and then I went home" in four words has told you where the weight is.

The third layer is the meaning the person has made: the conclusion they have drawn about themselves, about others, or about what is possible. This is the layer that most often needs revisiting, and it is the layer least likely to be volunteered, because the person does not experience it as an interpretation. They experience it as what the events proved.

A helper listening only at the first layer will produce accurate summaries and change very little. A helper who can hear all three has something to work with.

#### What Gets in the Way

There are three things I observe most often getting in the way of genuine listening.

The first is premature understanding. We form an interpretation of what the client means, and once we have formed it, we stop truly listening. Everything that follows is filtered through the interpretation we have already arrived at. A helper in this state is no longer attending to the client; they are confirming their own hypothesis.

The second is advice readiness. The moment a problem becomes legible, many helpers begin composing a response. The listening becomes a formality.

The client senses this, usually without being able to name it, and the result is a subtle withdrawal. They say less, and they say it less honestly.

The third is distraction by one's own experience. A client describes a situation that echoes something in the helper's own life, and the helper is suddenly partly elsewhere, partly managing their own material.

This is not a character fault. It is a human reflex. But it costs the client the quality of attention they came for.

#### What It Looks Like to Listen Well

A helper who is genuinely tuned in communicates that they are present. Not through technique, not through careful paraphrasing performed for effect, but through the quality of their attention. The client feels met, not observed.

Concretely, it means maintaining the kind of contact that invites the client to keep going. It means resisting the urge to finish sentences, to redirect, to insert your own frame over the one the client is building. It means allowing silence, because silence is often where the important material lives.

And it means responding in a way that shows you have heard not only the content but the feeling. Not by labelling the feeling for the client, which can feel presumptuous, but by reflecting what you have heard in a way that gives the client room to confirm or correct it.

There is a particular kind of silence worth learning to recognise. It is the pause that comes after a person has said something slightly more honest than they intended. It is short, and it is fragile, and the most common thing a helper does with it is fill it. Left alone, it is very often followed by the most useful sentence in the conversation.

#### Why This Cannot Be Faked

Helpers are sometimes taught listening as a set of visible behaviours: maintain eye contact, nod, paraphrase what you heard, do not interrupt. Each of those correlates with genuine attention, which is why they were noticed in the first place. None of them produces it.

A person performing the behaviours of listening while mentally composing their reply is a familiar experience to almost everyone who has been on the receiving end of it, and the giveaway is rarely anything you could point at. It is the quality of what comes back. A reply that was formed while you were still speaking answers the version of your problem that existed thirty seconds ago, and it lands slightly off, in a way that is hard to articulate and easy to feel.

This matters practically because it means listening cannot be improved by adding techniques on top of divided attention. The technique is downstream. What has to change is what you are doing with your own mind while the other person speaks, and the honest starting point is noticing how much of that time is currently spent on your own contribution.

There is a modest exercise that reveals this quickly. In your next conversation, resolve that you will not speak until you have silently named, to yourself, what the other person is feeling. Not what you think of it, not what you would suggest. Just the feeling.

Most people find they cannot do it, because they had not been tracking that at all.

#### What to Do With This

The clearest diagnostic I know is this: after a helping conversation, ask yourself how much you remember of what the client said, and how much you remember of what you said. If the balance tilts toward your own contributions, you were probably listening less well than you believed.

A second, harder test: can you name what the person felt, as distinct from what happened to them? If the only account you can give is a sequence of events, you heard the first layer and missed the two beneath it.

Developing genuine listening is slow work, and it requires honest self-observation.
